source_text: CAPUT DECIMUM, De Euangelio: ubi de Symbolo Apostolorum. Euangelium est verbum Dei annuncians & proponens omnibus hominibus apprehendendum Christum redemptorem cum meritis suis, & gratis promittens eum viva fide apprehendentibus propter eundem remissionem peccatorum, iustitiam & salutem aeternam. Euangelii, quod proprie significat bonum seu laetum nunciam, definitionem scite proponunt Theologi Leidenses synops. disp. 22 thesibus primis sex, & D. Lutherus. Notat in Theologia bonum nunciam de nato nobis salvatore Luc. 2:10-11 eiusque meritis; speciatim doctrinam de Christo redemptore & gratuita remissione peccatorum propter illum (Matth. 11:5; Rom. 1:16). Alias per synecdochen totam doctrinam N.T. quae etiam legem complectitur (Marc. 1:14-15).
english: CHAPTER TEN. On the Gospel: where also on the Apostles' Creed.

The Gospel is the word of God announcing and proposing to all humans Christ the Redeemer with His merits to be apprehended, and freely promising to those who apprehend Him by living faith remission of sins, righteousness, and eternal salvation for His sake.

Gospel properly means a good or glad message. In theology it notes the good news of the Savior born for us (Luke 2:10-11) and His merits; specially the doctrine of Christ the Redeemer and free remission of sins for Him (Matt. 11:5; Rom. 1:16). Sometimes by synecdoche it means the whole New Testament teaching, which also embraces the law (Mark 1:14-15).

source_text: Continet autem Euangelium tanquam materiam subiectam potissimum duo: 1. doctrinam de Christo salvatore hominum eiusque merito (Rom. 1:3)—ubi dogmata de incarnatione, impletione legis, solutione poenarum, liberatione a maledictione, reconciliatione cum Deo, superatione Diaboli; 2. doctrinam de applicatione meriti Christi, ubi agitur de remissione peccatorum (Acts 10:36, 43), de perfecta iustitia Christi nobis promissa (1 Cor. 1:30), de salute aeterna (Rom. 1:16; 1 Tim. 1:15).
english: The Gospel chiefly contains as subject-matter two things: 1. the doctrine of Christ the Savior of humans and His merit (Rom. 1:3)—incarnation, fulfillment of the law, payment of penalties, liberation from the curse, reconciliation with God, overthrow of the Devil;
2. the doctrine of applying Christ's merit—remission of sins (Acts 10:36, 43), perfect righteousness of Christ promised to us (1 Cor. 1:30), and eternal salvation (Rom. 1:16; 1 Tim. 1:15).

source_text: Differunt Lex & Euangelium 1. materia: lex praecipit opera; Euangelium annunciat Christum fide apprehendendum, unde dicitur lex fidei (Rom. 3:27) & auditus fidei (Gal. 3:2). 2. Forma: promissiones legis fiunt sub conditione proprii meriti (Lev. 18:5); Euangelii sunt gratuita (Rom. 4:16; Eph. 2:8)—verbum gratiae (Acts 20:24). 3. Effectis: lex terret & damnat (Rom. 3:20; 4:15); Euangelium consolatur & absolvit (Isa. 61:1-2; Luke 4:18)—Euangelium pacis (Eph. 6:15), verbum salutis. 4. Objecto: lex ad impios; Euangelium ad contrita corda (Matt. 11:28). 5. Modo patefactionis: lex natura nota (Rom. 2:15); Euangelium mysterium revelatum per Filium (John 1:18; Rom. 16:26; Col. 1:26).
english: Law and Gospel differ: 1. in matter—the law commands works; the Gospel announces Christ to be apprehended by faith (Rom. 3:27; Gal. 3:2);
2. in form—law-promises under condition of one's own merit (Lev. 18:5); Gospel-promises free (Rom. 4:16; Eph. 2:8);
3. in effects—the law terrifies and condemns (Rom. 3:20); the Gospel consoles and absolves (Isa. 61:1-2; Luke 4:18);
4. in object—the law toward the ungodly; the Gospel toward crushed hearts (Matt. 11:28);
5. in mode of revelation—the law somehow known by nature (Rom. 2:15); the Gospel a mystery revealed through the Son (John 1:18; Rom. 16:26).

source_text: Euangelium igitur non est doctrina operum, ideoque nec nova sive mandata sive consilia legi divinae superaddit. Non esse doctrinam operum patet ex Rom. 10. III. Compendium sive summula Euangelii est symbolum Apostolorum, cuius consideranda est litera, origo & auctoritas. IV. Literam harmonice dispositam sequens exhibet SCHEMA SUMMAE.
english: Therefore the Gospel is not a doctrine of works, and so adds neither new commands nor counsels upon the divine law. That it is not a doctrine of works is clear from Romans 10.

III. The compendium or little sum of the Gospel is the Apostles' Creed, whose letter, origin, and authority are to be considered. IV. Its letter, harmoniously arranged, the following SCHEMA of the sum exhibits.

source_text: V–VII. Symbolum ab initio baptismo in Trinitate ipsa sola consistebat, ut ex Martialem, Ignatio, Justino, Irenaeo, Tertulliano, Origene, Novatiano, & Nicaeno symbolo colligitur. Quotquot in antiquissimis patribus symboli expositiones extant, ultra Trinitatem nequaquam progrediuntur. VII. Quod hodieque est, quantum ad reliquas clausulas, nihil aliud continet quam splendidas quasi vestes primi illius corporis & exstructiones in illud fundamentum, quae suis temporibus necessario addebantur ad haereses exstinguendas & iam necessario retinentur ad impediendum ne recrudescant. Haeretici occasionem dederunt explicationis magis popularis illius symboli quod antea in maiestate quasi silentio complicatum fuerat.
english: V–VII. From the beginning the baptismal Creed consisted in the Trinity alone, as gathered from the earliest fathers and the Nicene Creed. Ancient expositions do not go beyond the Trinity.

VII. What the Creed is today, as to the remaining clauses, contains nothing but as it were splendid garments of that first body and fair structures upon that foundation, which in their times were necessarily added to extinguish heresies and are now necessarily retained lest they break out again. Heretics gave occasion for a more popular explanation of that Creed which before had been folded as in majesty of silence.

source_text: VIII. Auctoritas symboli Apostolorum consideratur vel illius quod fuit a principio, vel illius quale postmodum occasione diversarum haeresum explicatum est. IX. Symboli quod fuit a principio auctoritas est prorsus divina & reliquis canonicis scripturis aequalis. Nam immediate est a Jesu Christo Servatore nostro, Matth. 28:19. Sensum articulorum fidei pie docteque enarrarunt e junioribus Lutherus, Melanchthon, Erasmus, Bullingerus, Calvinus, Chytraeus, Hemmingius, Ursinus, Olevianus, Piscator, Perkinsus, Alstedius, alii. CAPUT UNDECIMUM sequitur, De sacramentis in genere.
english: VIII. The authority of the Apostles' Creed is considered either as it was from the beginning, or as it was later explained on the occasion of diverse heresies.

IX. The authority of the Creed as it was from the beginning is altogether divine and equal to the other canonical Scriptures, for it is immediately from Jesus Christ our Savior (Matt. 28:19). Among juniors Luther, Melanchthon, Erasmus, Bullinger, Calvin, Chytraeus, Hemmingius, Ursinus, Olevianus, Piscator, Perkins, Alsted, and others have piously and learnedly expounded the sense of the articles.
CHAPTER ELEVEN follows, On the sacraments in general.
